newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Tearful defendant pleads for life in Vietnam trial.
newsitem.headline: Tearful defendant pleads for life in Vietnam trial.

text.p: The lead defendant in Vietnam's biggest corruption trial broke down in tears and pleaded for his life before judges retired on Thursday to consider their verdicts.

State papers carried photographs of Pham Huy Phuoc, former head of Communist Party-affiliated firm Tamexco, holding a handkerchief to his face as defence lawyers made their final arguments for leniency on Wednesday.
They said a death sentence for Phuoc, as called for by state prosecutors, would orphan his three children and leave his elderly mother with no means of support.
But in Thursday's official media there was little sign the appeal for life might be heeded.

The Saigon Times Daily led its coverage with a politburo directive demonstrating Hanoi's resolve to stamp out graft by asking district leaders, civil servants and managers of state firms to declare their assets.

"Judicial agencies must strictly deal with corrupt officials and firmly screen the State machinery," it said. "In the short run they will have to seriously tackle notorious corruption cases known to the general public."
The article went on to quote statistics for the number of corruption cases which have been brought before courts in recent years as a result of the efforts of the authorities.
The Tamexco trial has become a showcase for Hanoi's anti-graft resolve, and centres around allegations that Phuoc and others connived to siphon off millions of dollars in state money.
In addition to calls for the death sentence for Phuoc, prosecutors have called for three others to face the firing squad and a range of jail terms for the 16 other defendants.
However, local newspapers said no verdict was being made in connection with banking documents showing alleged links between the case and Vietcombank, Vietnam's biggest state-owned commercial bank.
Tamexco is a Ho Chi Minh City trading company. Several of those implicated in the case have close links to some of the most powerful people in Vietnam.
Despite widespread coverage in the domestic media, foreign journalists have not been allowed to attend the trial.
Final verdicts are expected late on Friday.
